quests.question: The woman who is standing by the door is my aunt. Which of these means exactly the same thing, in reduced form?
quests.hint: Drop both the relative pronoun and the verb 'is,' keeping only the '-ing' form.
quests.explanation: 'Standing' is the reduced form of 'who is standing': the subject relative pronoun and the auxiliary 'is' are dropped, leaving just the present participle.
options: The woman stood by the door is my aunt.
The woman who standing by the door is my aunt.
The woman stand by the door is my aunt.
The woman standing by the door is my aunt.
quests.correctAnswer: The woman standing by the door is my aunt.

quests.question: Full: 'The passengers who were waiting at the gate grew impatient.' Reduced: 'The passengers ___ at the gate grew impatient.'
quests.hint: The full clause describes an ongoing action ('were waiting') - which participle captures that?
quests.explanation: 'Waiting' is correct: it reduces 'who were waiting,' dropping the pronoun and the auxiliary 'were,' leaving the present participle.
options: wait
waiting
who waiting
waited
quests.correctAnswer: waiting

quests.question: Which sentence can be correctly reduced using an '-ing' form?
quests.hint: Check who is doing the preparing in each sentence - is the antecedent itself performing the action?
quests.explanation: Only subject relative clauses reduce with '-ing': the chef is doing the preparing. In the other case, 'I' is doing the preparing, not 'the dish,' so that object relative clause cannot be reduced this way.
options: The dish that I am preparing for the party is a family recipe.
Neither sentence can be reduced.
The chef who is preparing the tasting menu trained in Paris.
Both sentences can be reduced the same way.
quests.correctAnswer: The chef who is preparing the tasting menu trained in Paris.

quests.question: The car that was stolen last night was found this morning. Which of these means exactly the same thing, in reduced form?
quests.hint: Drop both the relative pronoun and the verb 'was,' keeping only the past participle.
quests.explanation: 'Stolen' is the reduced form of 'that was stolen': the pronoun and the auxiliary 'was' are dropped, leaving just the past participle - correct because the original clause was passive.
options: The car stealing last night was found this morning.
The car that stolen last night was found this morning.
The car steal last night was found this morning.
The car stolen last night was found this morning.
quests.correctAnswer: The car stolen last night was found this morning.

quests.question: Full: 'The documents that were signed yesterday need to be filed.' Reduced: 'The documents ___ yesterday need to be filed.'
quests.hint: The full clause is passive ('were signed') - which participle matches a passive meaning?
quests.explanation: 'Signed' is correct: it reduces 'that were signed,' dropping the pronoun and 'were,' leaving the past participle.
options: signed
that signed
sign
signing
quests.correctAnswer: signed

quests.question: Which sentence correctly uses a reduced clause to show that the report was WRITTEN BY someone else?
quests.hint: The report didn't write itself - someone wrote it. Which participle form shows this passive relationship correctly?
quests.explanation: 'Written' (past participle) correctly shows the passive meaning; '-ing' would incorrectly suggest the report itself is actively writing something.
options: The report that written by the intern contained several errors.
The report write by the intern contained several errors.
The report written by the intern contained several errors.
The report writing the summary contained several errors.
quests.correctAnswer: The report written by the intern contained several errors.

quests.question: Compare: A) 'The employee managing the project...' B) 'The employee managed by the project...' Which one describes an employee who is IN CHARGE of the project?
quests.hint: Ask whether the employee is performing the managing, or receiving it - and whether that second reading even makes sense.
quests.explanation: 'Managing' shows the employee is doing the managing - in charge of the project. 'Managed by the project' would be an odd passive, since projects don't typically manage people.
options: Neither sentence
Both sentences equally
Sentence A
Sentence B
quests.correctAnswer: Sentence A

quests.question: The negotiations ___ by both sides finally reached a resolution.
quests.hint: Were the negotiations doing the leading, or being led by the two sides?
quests.explanation: 'Led' is correct because the negotiations were led BY both sides - a passive relationship; '-ing' would wrongly suggest the negotiations themselves were actively leading something.
options: that leading
led
leading
lead
quests.correctAnswer: led

quests.question: Which sentence correctly describes a student who FEELS curious about the topic, rather than one who causes curiosity in others?
quests.hint: One of these participles describes how the student feels; the other describes the effect the student has on other people.
quests.explanation: 'Interested' describes the student's own feeling. 'Interesting' would describe a student who causes interest in others - a different meaning entirely.
options: The interest student asked several follow-up questions.
Both sentences mean the same thing.
The interested student asked several follow-up questions.
The interesting student asked several follow-up questions.
quests.correctAnswer: The interested student asked several follow-up questions.

quests.question: Which sentence CANNOT be correctly reduced using a participle?
quests.hint: Check whether the antecedent is doing the action, or receiving it from someone else mentioned in the clause.
quests.explanation: 'The photographer' - not 'the pictures' - is doing the taking, so this is an object relative clause; object relative clauses generally cannot be reduced to a simple participle this way, unlike subject relative clauses.
options: The photographer who is taking the pictures arrived early.
The pictures that the photographer is taking will be ready tomorrow.
Both sentences can be reduced the same way.
Neither sentence can be reduced.
quests.correctAnswer: The pictures that the photographer is taking will be ready tomorrow.

quests.question: Which sentence sounds unnatural if reduced with an '-ing' form, because the verb describes a mental state rather than an ongoing action?
quests.hint: Compare 'waiting,' which describes an ongoing action, with 'knowing,' which describes a mental state - does the second sound natural in everyday speech?
quests.explanation: Stative verbs like 'know,' 'believe,' or 'want' generally resist this kind of reduction, even though the '-ing' form technically exists; 'waiting' reduces naturally, but 'knowing' sounds stiff or archaic here.
options: The man who knows the answer raised his hand.
The man who is waiting outside is my neighbor.
Both reduce equally naturally.
Neither reduces naturally.
quests.correctAnswer: The man who knows the answer raised his hand.

quests.question: Which sentence CANNOT be reduced to a shorter participle phrase?
quests.hint: Reduction works by dropping a relative pronoun and a form of 'be' - does 'whose' behave the same way as 'who' or 'that' here?
quests.explanation: Clauses beginning with 'whose' generally cannot be shortened to a simple participle phrase, because 'whose' shows possession, not simply a subject doing or receiving an action.
options: The employee whose contract is being reviewed raised concerns.
The employee who is reviewing the contract found an error.
Neither can be reduced.
Both can be reduced the same way.
quests.correctAnswer: The employee whose contract is being reviewed raised concerns.

quests.question: Why can't 'The man whose car was stolen' be reduced to something like 'The man car stolen'?
quests.hint: Think about what job 'whose' is doing in this sentence - what would be lost if it disappeared?
quests.explanation: 'Whose' shows that the car belongs to the man; removing it would destroy that link, leaving a nonsensical string of nouns. This differs from 'who' or 'that,' which can be dropped because the participle alone still shows the relationship to the antecedent.
options: Because 'stolen' can only be used with 'that,' never with 'whose.'
Because 'whose' clauses are always non-defining.
Because possessive clauses never contain a verb.
Because dropping 'whose' would break the possessive link between the man and the car, leaving the sentence unclear.
quests.correctAnswer: Because dropping 'whose' would break the possessive link between the man and the car, leaving the sentence unclear.

quests.question: Which sentence correctly keeps 'whose' unreduced, as required?
quests.hint: Only one of these keeps the possessive link between the company and its profits clear and grammatical.
quests.explanation: 'Whose' must stay to show that the profits belong to the company; none of the other options preserve both the meaning and the grammar.
options: The company declined profits announced layoffs.
The company profits declined announced layoffs.
The company whose declined profits announced layoffs.
The company whose profits declined announced layoffs.
quests.correctAnswer: The company whose profits declined announced layoffs.

quests.question: The company whose profits declined announced layoffs affecting workers across three states. Which part of this sentence IS a valid reduction?
quests.hint: Look for a participle phrase elsewhere in the sentence that stands in for a full relative clause, separate from the 'whose' clause.
quests.explanation: 'Affecting workers across three states' is a reduced form of 'that affected workers...' - a valid reduction, unlike the 'whose' clause earlier in the sentence, which must stay in full.
options: The company
affecting workers across three states
whose profits declined
announced layoffs
quests.correctAnswer: affecting workers across three states

quests.question: My brother, who lives in Paris, works as a chef. Can this non-defining clause also be reduced?
quests.hint: Try applying the same drop-the-pronoun-and-'be' pattern you've used before, but keep the commas this time.
quests.explanation: Non-defining clauses can be reduced too, as long as the commas stay in place: 'living in Paris' replaces 'who lives in Paris,' with the extra information still clearly set off by commas.
options: No, non-defining clauses can never be reduced.
No, because 'lives' cannot form a participle.
Yes, but only if the comma is removed first.
Yes: 'My brother, living in Paris, works as a chef.'
quests.correctAnswer: Yes: 'My brother, living in Paris, works as a chef.'

quests.question: The bridge, which was built in 1932, connects the two districts. Which reduced version is correct?
quests.hint: Keep the commas exactly where they were, and choose the participle form that matches the passive meaning of 'was built.'
quests.explanation: 'Built' correctly reduces 'which was built,' and the commas must stay since this is still non-defining information about a unique bridge.
options: The bridge, that built in 1932, connects the two districts.
The bridge, built in 1932, connects the two districts.
The bridge built in 1932 connects the two districts.
The bridge, building in 1932, connects the two districts.
quests.correctAnswer: The bridge, built in 1932, connects the two districts.

quests.question: Which sentence commits an error by losing its commas during reduction?
quests.hint: Ask whether 'Mount Everest' needs any narrowing down at all - and whether the comma should have stayed even after reduction.
quests.explanation: Reducing a clause doesn't remove the need for its commas; since Mount Everest is unique, the non-defining comma must stay even in the reduced form.
options: Mount Everest, standing at over 8,800 meters, is the tallest mountain on Earth.
Mount Everest standing at over 8,800 meters is the tallest mountain on Earth.
The password, which was reset yesterday, no longer works.
The volunteers, working through the night, finished just before dawn.
quests.correctAnswer: Mount Everest standing at over 8,800 meters is the tallest mountain on Earth.

quests.question: The team managing the crisis worked around the clock. What is the FULL, unreduced meaning of 'managing the crisis'?
quests.hint: Ask whether the team is doing the managing, or whether something else is managing the team.
quests.explanation: 'Managing' is a present participle showing an active relationship: the team was doing the managing. The full form is 'who was/were managing the crisis.'
options: who was managing the crisis / who were managing the crisis
whose crisis was being managed
that the crisis was managing
who was being managed by the crisis
quests.correctAnswer: who was managing the crisis / who were managing the crisis

quests.question: The employees selected for the pilot program will start Monday. What is the FULL, unreduced meaning of 'selected for the pilot program'?
quests.hint: Ask whether the employees chose the program, or whether someone else chose the employees for it.
quests.explanation: 'Selected' is a past participle showing a passive relationship: someone else selected the employees. The full form is 'who were selected for the pilot program.'
options: who are selecting the pilot program
who selected the pilot program
whose pilot program was selected
who were selected for the pilot program
quests.correctAnswer: who were selected for the pilot program

quests.question: Compare: A) 'The horse racing down the track was disqualified.' B) 'The horse raced down the track was disqualified.' Which one means the horse itself was running?
quests.hint: One participle shows the horse doing the running; the other would need someone racing the horse, which is a less natural reading here.
quests.explanation: 'Racing' (active) means the horse itself was running down the track. 'Raced' would suggest someone raced the horse, a less natural reading in this context.
options: Both sentences
Sentence A
Sentence B
Neither sentence
quests.correctAnswer: Sentence A

quests.question: Which is the correct reduced form of 'The workers who are striking for better pay have blocked the entrance'?
quests.hint: Drop 'who are' and keep only the participle that matches the ongoing action.
quests.explanation: 'Striking' correctly reduces 'who are striking,' dropping the pronoun and 'are.'
options: The workers struck for better pay have blocked the entrance.
The workers who striking for better pay have blocked the entrance.
The workers striking for better pay have blocked the entrance.
The workers strike for better pay have blocked the entrance.
quests.correctAnswer: The workers striking for better pay have blocked the entrance.

quests.question: Which is the correct reduced form of 'The evidence that was presented in court convinced the jury'?
quests.hint: This clause is passive ('was presented') - which participle form matches that?
quests.explanation: 'Presented' correctly reduces 'that was presented,' dropping the pronoun and 'was,' matching the passive meaning.
options: The evidence present in court convinced the jury.
The evidence that presented in court convinced the jury.
The evidence presented in court convinced the jury.
The evidence presenting in court convinced the jury.
quests.correctAnswer: The evidence presented in court convinced the jury.

quests.question: Which is the correct reduced form of 'The book that my sister is reading was a birthday gift'?
quests.hint: Ask who is actually doing the reading - the book, or someone else mentioned in the clause?
quests.explanation: Since 'my sister' - not 'the book' - is doing the reading, this is an object relative clause and cannot be reduced to a simple participle phrase attached to 'book.' Note: dropping 'that' to get 'the book my sister is reading' is a different technique - object relative pronoun omission - not participle reduction.
options: This clause cannot be reduced to a participle phrase, because 'my sister,' not 'the book,' is doing the reading.
The book reads by my sister was a birthday gift.
The book my sister reading was a birthday gift.
The book reading by my sister was a birthday gift.
quests.correctAnswer: This clause cannot be reduced to a participle phrase, because 'my sister,' not 'the book,' is doing the reading.

quests.question: Expand this reduced clause to its full form: 'The technicians repairing the server worked through lunch.'
quests.hint: The reduced participle 'repairing' suggests an ongoing action - which full verb tense best captures that?
quests.explanation: 'Repairing' most naturally expands to the past progressive 'who were repairing,' matching the ongoing nature of the action alongside 'worked through lunch.'
options: The technicians who repair the server worked through lunch.
The technicians who repaired the server worked through lunch.
The technicians who were repairing the server worked through lunch.
The technicians whose server was repaired worked through lunch.
quests.correctAnswer: The technicians who were repairing the server worked through lunch.

quests.question: Expand this reduced clause to its full form: 'The applications submitted after the deadline were rejected automatically.'
quests.hint: 'Submitted' is a past participle - applications don't submit themselves, so which voice does the full clause need?
quests.explanation: 'Submitted' expands to the passive 'that were submitted,' since applications are submitted by someone, not by themselves.
options: The applications that are submitting after the deadline were rejected automatically.
The applications whose deadline was submitted were rejected automatically.
The applications that submitted after the deadline were rejected automatically.
The applications that were submitted after the deadline were rejected automatically.
quests.correctAnswer: The applications that were submitted after the deadline were rejected automatically.

quests.question: Expand this reduced clause to its full form, keeping the meaning and punctuation the same: 'The new policy, announced without warning, upset many employees.'
quests.hint: Keep both commas exactly where they are, and choose the pronoun and voice that match the passive participle 'announced.'
quests.explanation: 'Announced' expands to 'which was announced,' and since this is non-defining information, both commas and 'which' (not 'that') must be used.
options: The new policy, which was announced without warning, upset many employees.
The new policy, that was announced without warning, upset many employees.
The new policy, announcing without warning, upset many employees.
The new policy which was announced without warning upset many employees.
quests.correctAnswer: The new policy, which was announced without warning, upset many employees.

quests.question: Which sentence correctly describes documents that SOMEONE ELSE reviewed, rather than documents that were reviewing anything?
quests.hint: The documents didn't review anything themselves - someone reviewed them. Which participle shows this correctly?
quests.explanation: 'Reviewed' (past participle) correctly shows the passive relationship: the auditor reviewed the documents. '-ing' would reverse the roles entirely.
options: The documents review by the auditor revealed inconsistencies.
The documents reviewed by the auditor revealed inconsistencies.
Both sentences mean the same thing.
The documents reviewing the auditor revealed inconsistencies.
quests.correctAnswer: The documents reviewed by the auditor revealed inconsistencies.

quests.question: Which sentence correctly combines these facts, keeping the 'whose' clause intact: 'The novelist has a new book. The novelist's earlier work won critical acclaim. The novelist is currently touring five countries.'
quests.hint: The 'whose' clause must stay in full; only check whether the rest of the sentence is logically and grammatically combined.
quests.explanation: 'Whose earlier work won critical acclaim' correctly keeps the possessive clause intact and unreduced, while the rest of the sentence combines the remaining facts clearly.
options: The novelist, whose earlier work won critical acclaim, is currently touring five countries with a new book.
The novelist earlier work won critical acclaim touring five countries with a new book.
The novelist, earlier work winning critical acclaim, is currently touring five countries with a new book.
The novelist whose winning critical acclaim earlier work is currently touring five countries with a new book.
quests.correctAnswer: The novelist, whose earlier work won critical acclaim, is currently touring five countries with a new book.

quests.question: Which sentence contains an error related to reduced relative clauses?
quests.hint: A reduced clause drops its relative pronoun entirely - check whether any option has accidentally kept one.
quests.explanation: 'The house who belonging to my uncle' incorrectly keeps 'who' alongside the reduced participle 'belonging'; a reduced clause never keeps its relative pronoun.
options: The house who belonging to my uncle is for sale.
The bridge, built in 1932, connects the two districts.
The manager reviewing the applications will call finalists tomorrow.
The evidence presented in court convinced the jury.
quests.correctAnswer: The house who belonging to my uncle is for sale.
